lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Cerberus, my friend! Since we’re practically family—me being a 'Dog' philosopher and all—tell me, by the Styx: what was Socrates actually like when he came down here? I assume, being a god, you can speak like a human when you want to, not just bark.

lines.speaker: Cerberus
lines.text: From a distance, Menippus, he seemed perfectly unflappable. He approached without a flicker of fear, clearly wanting to put on a good show for the audience standing outside the cavern. But the moment he peered into the chasm and saw the pitch black... [chuckles] he hesitated. The hemlock was making his legs a bit sluggish, so I gave him a little nip on the foot and dragged him down. He bawled like a baby. Wailing about his children, completely falling to pieces.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: [laughs] So the man was just a fraud! He wasn't actually indifferent to death at all?

lines.speaker: Cerberus
lines.text: Not exactly. He just saw it was inevitable, so he put on a brave face, pretending to welcome what he was going to suffer anyway—just to get a round of applause from the spectators. Honestly, it's the same story with all of them: bold and brave right up to the threshold. What happens inside is the real test.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: And what about me? How did I look when I came down?

lines.speaker: Cerberus
lines.text: You were the only one, Menippus—well, you and Diogenes before you—who acted worthy of the breed. You didn't have to be forced. Nobody pushed you. You walked in voluntarily, laughing, and telling the rest of the world they could go hang.
